newsitem.title: GERMANY: Shadow of budget row to loom over FDP congress.
newsitem.headline: Shadow of budget row to loom over FDP congress.

text.p: Germany's liberal Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners, gather this week for a party congress likely to be dominated by the search for ways to plug a huge gap in government finances.

The party, which provides Kohl's centre-right alliance with its 12-seat parliamentary majority, has styled itself as the champion of lower taxes but now faces pressure to agree to a tax hike to fill a projected budget shortfall of 18 billion marks ($10.5 billion).

FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt has repeatedly opposed a rise in fuel tax or value-added tax -- two options Finance Minister Theo Waigel has not ruled out as he battles to meet the entry criteria for Europe's planned single currency.
"The money Waigel doesn't have for 1997 can't be brought in by tax rises anyway. It's far too late in the year for that," honorary FDP chairman Otto Lambsdorff said on Wednesday.
"The only way to get it is by making savings and probably also by revaluing the gold reserves at the Bundesbank."
Gerhardt has said he will emphasise the party's opposition to tax rises when he opens the three-day FDP congress in the central town of Wiesbaden on Friday.
The FDP's stance will be reinforced if delegates approve an emergency motion, planned by a regional branch, calling for the party to commit itself not to sanction a rise in fuel tax.

The FDP can ill afford another blow to its tax-cutting credentials. Their image suffered a dent last year when Kohl's government postponed a cut in the "solidarity surcharge" imposed on income tax to help pay for German unification.

Congress delegates are expected to approve a set of "Wiesbaden Principles" stressing the FDP's commitment to cut the powers of the state and including a long-term plan to force all levels of public administration to pass balanced budgets.

The party, engaged in a permanent struggle to overcome the five-percent barrier required to be represented in parliament, will also try to broaden its appeal by devoting debates at the congress to issues such as education and unemployment.

"The FDP today is a neoliberal party of the market economy which does not have enough committed voters to get more than five percent. That's exactly where the FDP's problem lies," political scientist Professor Peter Loesche said.
The FDP's decision to concentrate on economic issues over the last few years has disappointed both the party's traditional pro-human rights left wing and its nationalist fringe.

One member of nationalist group, Heiner Kappel, plans to challenge Gerhardt for the leadership during the congress. Party members say Kappel could view a score of more than 10 percent of the vote as a success.
Loesche said he did not believe the congress would give the FDP significant new impetus.
"The programme will bring in some new aspects but, seen from the outside, the FDP appears again and again very clearly as a party of tax-cutting and neoliberalism," he told German Radio.
"It contested three state elections on this basis early last year and was relatively successful but whether that will continue in the future is highly questionable."
